analysis.one_liner: Blocks federal fracking rules on federal lands in states with their own fracking rules.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have barred federal fracking rules on federal land in states with any fracking rules of their own, drew two Republican cosponsors and died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the Interior Department from enforcing any federal rule, guidance, or permit requirement on hydraulic fracturing on or under land in any state that has its own fracking rules, and would have required federal officials to follow state rules even when those rules are weaker or do not meet federal requirements. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies drilling on land owned by the federal government would gain the most: in any state with its own fracking rules, they would face no federal fracking regulations at all, and federal officials would have to accept the state's rules even if they were less restrictive or did not meet federal requirements. Geothermal producers on federal land would get the same treatment. States would also gain sole regulatory control over fracking on federal land within their borders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal land

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits the Interior Department from enforcing any federal regulation, guidance, or permit requirement on hydraulic fracturing on or under land in any state that has its own fracking regulations or permit requirements.

It requires the Interior Department to defer to state fracking rules on federal land 'regardless of whether' those rules are duplicative, more or less restrictive, or do not meet federal requirements — so a state's weaker rules would displace federal standards entirely.
It covers not just the fracking itself but 'any component' of the process, and applies to oil, gas, and geothermal production on federal land.

analysis.who_pays: The public that owns the federal lands would bear the cost. Federal land is national land, but drilling safeguards would be set solely by whichever state the land sits in, and the bill explicitly allows state rules that fail to meet federal requirements to take their place. People living near federal-land wells and relying on groundwater would lose a uniform federal baseline of fracking oversight.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not just avoid duplicate regulation — it removes any federal floor. Interior would have to defer to state rules even when they 'do not meet Federal regulations, guidance, or permit requirements,' so a state with minimal standards could set the only rules for fracking on federal land inside it.

Federal lands belong to all Americans, but under the bill only the host state's rules would apply, leaving no federal backstop for water, air, or land impacts of fracking on property owned by the nation as a whole.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: There is a real argument for the bill: states have long been the primary regulators of drilling, they are closer to operations, and overlapping state and federal permitting can duplicate paperwork. But the bill goes well beyond harmonizing rules — it requires federal deference even where state rules are less restrictive or fail to meet federal requirements, which would eliminate a federal baseline on land owned by all Americans. The cost to public-land safeguards outweighs the administrative convenience.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Orrin Hatch introduced the bill on February 6, 2017, with Senator John Barrasso, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day.

The bill would have amended the Mineral Leasing Act to bar the Interior Department from enforcing any federal fracking rule on land in states with their own fracking rules, and to require deference to state rules even when they do not meet federal requirements.
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, federal authority to set fracking standards on federal land was left intact and no industry gained the exemption it sought. The outcome mostly preserved the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; federal fracking authority preserved

for.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to replace federal fracking rules on federal land with state rules.

for.name: Sen. John Barrasso
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's co-introducer at introduction.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee (Chair Lisa Murkowski)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had only Republican sponsorship — Hatch, Barrasso, and two Republican cosponsors total — and no vote was ever held, so the partisan shape of the full Senate was never tested.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies drilling on federal land
industries.note: The bill would have freed these operators from any federal fracking regulation in states with their own rules, even weaker ones, on land owned by the federal government. Their gain comes directly from removing a federal oversight baseline that protects water and public land.
The bill extends the same state-displacement rule to geothermal production activities on federal land, removing federal permit requirements for fracking components of geothermal development.
